notes:
Here are verse-by-verse notes on Psalm 135. My searches didn't turn up everything you asked for, so I've listed the gaps first.

**What I couldn't find:**
- **Modern scholarship sites:** nothing from bibleodyssey.org, and no netbible.org translators' notes. The only scholarly-style notes I found are on sources and dating, from older commentaries. The NET wording comes from translation tables on biblehub.
- **Catholic and Orthodox:** only Augustine (on newadvent.org). Nothing from catholic.com or oca.org.
- **Protestant traditions:** no Lutheran, Pentecostal or Wesleyan (wesley.nnu.edu, seedbed) source that takes its own stand on a verse. The nearest to a Methodist voice is Adam Clarke.
- **Popular modern teaching:** nothing on prosperity, word of faith or hyper-grace readings of this psalm.

**The whole psalm**
- Almost every verse borrows from elsewhere in Scripture. Maclaren says the poet arranged familiar passages "in a new bouquet." https://biblehub.com/commentaries/expositors/psalms/135.htm
- Kidner's well-known remark: "Every verse of this psalm either echoes, quotes or is quoted by some other part of Scripture." https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/dcc/psalms-135.html
- **Date (older commentaries):** Clarke thinks the psalm was written after the exile. He passes on Calmet's guess that it was used at the dedication of the second temple. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/clarke/psalms/135.htm
- Constable says it is linked to one of the great feasts, but nobody knows which one. https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/dcc/psalms-135.html

**v. 1**
- "The name of the LORD" means God himself: his character and all his attributes. Gill gives the list. https://www.studylight.org/commentary/psalms/135-1.html
- Guzik adds that a name stood for a person's nature. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/psalm-135/
- Augustine: servants should praise God, and even more so servants who will one day gain the privilege of sons. https://www.newadvent.org/fathers/1801135.htm

**v. 2**
- **Who is being addressed?**
  - The Geneva Bible notes take "the house" to mean the Levites, and "the courts" to mean the ordinary people. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/gsb/psalms/135.htm
  - Keil & Delitzsch say these are not just the official temple staff (as in Psalm 134) but all who fear God. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/psalms/135-1.htm
  - Maclaren agrees that adding "courts" brings the people in too. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/expositors/psalms/135.htm
  - Calvin thinks the priests are addressed first, since they led the singing, with the people next. https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/cal/psalms-135.html
- Augustine: be thankful, because you were without, and you stand within. https://www.newadvent.org/fathers/1801135.htm

**v. 3**
- Two reasons to praise: God is good, and praise is pleasant. Benson (in the biblehub collection) gives both. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/psalms/135-1.htm
- Clarke gives the same two reasons. https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/acc/psalms-135.html
- **What is "pleasant"? Readers differ:**
  - Maclaren says it is the act of praising, as in Psalm 147:1, not the Name itself. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/expositors/psalms/135.htm
  - Spurgeon says the adjective may apply to the singing and to the name—they are both pleasant. https://www.blueletterbible.org/Comm/spurgeon_charles/tod/ps135.cfm
- Guzik: it's fine that worship is pleasant, but that should never be the main reason we worship. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/psalm-135/
- Augustine reads it as "He is sweet" and ties it to Christ the Mediator. https://www.newadvent.org/fathers/1801135.htm

**v. 4**
- The wording echoes Deuteronomy 7:6. God chose Israel because he loves them, not because they were great (Deuteronomy 7:7–8). The Hebrew *segullah* means a king's private, carefully kept treasure. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/psalm-135/
- **Calvin (Reformed):** God chose Israel and passed over the rest of the world. That proves the choice came from God's free mercy, not from anything good in Israel. https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/cal/psalms-135.html
- **Spurgeon (Baptist):** stresses what Israel was chosen *for*: to be the trustees of his truth, the maintainers of his worship, the mirrors of his mercy. https://archive.spurgeon.org/treasury/ps135.php
- **Applying it to Christians:** Horne (quoted by Guzik) says Christians are chosen in the same way. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/psalm-135/
- A Restoration-movement commentary says God's people today are the New Israel which is the Church. https://studylight.org/commentaries/eng/onr/psalms-135.html

**v. 5**
- Two names for God are used: "the LORD" (Yahweh, Israel's covenant God) and "our Lord" (Adonai, the Master of all). https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/psalm-135/
- The "I" in "I know" is emphatic in the Hebrew. Spurgeon notes that the psalmist knew it "by observation, inspiration, and realization." https://www.blueletterbible.org/Comm/spurgeon_charles/tod/ps135.cfm
- Calvin: "gods" is used only as a concession, because these are empty fictions. God's greatness simply outshines them. https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/cal/psalms-135.html

**v. 6**
This is the verse where Reformed and Baptist teachers press hardest on God's control. I found no Wesleyan or Arminian writer arguing back.
- **Calvin:** nothing happens by chance. He rejects the idea of a God who only keeps general order. In his words, nothing happens without, the divine will and decree. https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/cal/psalms-135.html
- **John Piper (Desiring God):** God is never forced into doing something he hates. In some sense he takes pleasure in everything he does, including the cross. https://www.desiringgod.org/articles/psalm-135-and-the-pleasure-of-god-in-all-he-does
- **Matthew Henry:** God does what he pleases because he pleases, and gives not an account of any of his matters. https://www.blueletterbible.org/Comm/mhc/Psa/Psa_135.cfm
- **Adam Clarke (Methodist):** puts it differently. Whatever God does is right and so pleases him, and he acts from his free will, not from any necessity. He doesn't talk about decrees. https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/acc/psalms-135.html
- **Geneva notes:** the psalmist ties God's power to his will, so that readers don't separate the two. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/gsb/psalms/135.htm

**v. 7**
- The verse is drawn from Jeremiah 10:13 and 51:16. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/expositors/psalms/135.htm
- It lifts Yahweh above Baal, the Canaanite weather god who was often pictured holding lightning. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/psalm-135/
- Calvin: rain is not "blind" nature at work but God's decree each time. https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/cal/psalms-135.html
- Spurgeon says much the same: It is the Lord who causes them to rise, and not a mere law. https://archive.spurgeon.org/treasury/ps135.php

**vv. 8–9**
- The last plague, the death of the firstborn, stands for all of God's "signs and wonders." https://www.blueletterbible.org/Comm/jfb/Psa/Psa_135.cfm
- Calvin: the psalmist starts with this plague, out of order, to show how much God cared about keeping his people safe. https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/cal/psalms-135.html
- Spurgeon calls the plague just punishment, because Egypt had drowned Israel's babies. He also notes that Pharaoh's officials were punished as his accomplices. https://archive.spurgeon.org/treasury/ps135.php
- Horne: Egypt was where Israel's God and the pagan gods fought it out. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/psalm-135/

**vv. 10–12**
- The land was conquered by God's power, not Israel's. https://www.blueletterbible.org/Comm/jfb/Psa/Psa_135.cfm
- Sihon and Og are named because they blocked the way into the land and were the first enemies Israel met. https://www.blueletterbible.org/Comm/spurgeon_charles/tod/ps135.cfm
- Spurgeon: God had promised Abraham the land long before. He let the Amorites stay there until their sin was "full." https://archive.spurgeon.org/treasury/ps135.php

**v. 13**
- God doesn't change. Boice and VanGemeren are both quoted on this, and VanGemeren adds that the meaning of God's name grew as he revealed more of himself. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/psalm-135/
- The wording echoes Exodus 3:15. https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/hsw/psalms-135.html
- Augustine looks back over creation and the Exodus, and in joy says that God's Name lasts forever. https://www.newadvent.org/fathers/1801135.htm

**v. 14**
- This is a quotation of Deuteronomy 32:36. It is also cited in Hebrews 10:30. https://biblehub.com/psalms/135-14.htm
- **Translations vary.** Older ones say "repent himself." The Douay-Rheims (Catholic) says "will be entreated in favour of his servants." https://www.studylight.org/bible/eng/nrs/psalms/135-14.html
- **What "repent" means here:**
  - Barnes: God acts *as if* he changed his mind. It is language suited to human weakness. https://www.studylight.org/bible/eng/nrs/psalms/135-14.html
  - The Pulpit Commentary: after enough discipline God relents. The book of Judges shows the pattern. https://biblehub.com/psalms/135-14.htm
- Coffman warns against Israel's assumption that God would rescue them however much they rebelled. https://www.studylight.org/commentary/psalms/135-14.html

**vv. 15–18**
- This section is taken from Psalm 115:4–8. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/psalm-135/
- **Verse 17 changes Psalm 115.** Where Psalm 115 says idols have noses but cannot smell, this psalm says there is no breath in their mouths. Maclaren explains the wordplay: the Hebrew word for "yea" is spelled like "nose," and "breath" sounds like "smell." https://biblehub.com/commentaries/expositors/psalms/135.htm
- **Verse 18:** idol makers become like their idols, spiritually dead. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/psalm-135/
- The Geneva notes say the passage warns God's own people against the same sin. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/gsb/psalms/135.htm
- **Protestant polemic against Catholics:**
  - A biblehub summary says Reformers used vv. 15-18 to expose the folly of relic worship. https://biblehub.com/chaptersummaries/psalms/135.htm
  - Spurgeon quotes Trapp attacking Catholic images. https://www.blueletterbible.org/Comm/spurgeon_charles/tod/ps135.cfm
  - Spurgeon also turns verse 18 against a baptismal regeneration which does not renew the nature. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/psalms/135-15.htm
  - These are one-sided Baptist positions. I found no Catholic, Lutheran or Anglican reply.
- Spurgeon also quotes a reminder that greed is idolatry too. https://www.blueletterbible.org/Comm/spurgeon_charles/tod/ps135.cfm

**vv. 19–20**
- These verses follow Psalm 115:9–11. Two changes: "house of Levi" is added, and "bless" replaces "trust." https://biblehub.com/commentaries/expositors/psalms/135.htm
- "You who fear the LORD" probably includes Gentile converts. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/psalm-135/
- Augustine's reading: Israel stands for the nations in general, Aaron for leaders, and Levi for servants. "You who fear the Lord" covers everyone else. He takes the true house of Israel to be Abraham's children by faith. https://www.newadvent.org/fathers/1801135.htm

**v. 21**
- This verse reverses the end of Psalm 134. There, blessing comes out of Zion to the people; here, the people bless God from Zion. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/expositors/psalms/135.htm
- Guzik: God is not a local god, and his greatness reaches beyond Zion. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/psalm-135/
- Augustine: while we live in hope we are "in Zion." At the end we will live in the eternal Jerusalem. https://www.newadvent.org/fathers/1801135.htm
